primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Severe renal microvascular injury and markedly reduced cortical perfusion, often in obstetric catastrophe, sepsis, or disseminated intravascular coagulation, can cause ischemic necrosis of renal cortical tissue with relative sparing of the medulla.
vignette: A 31-year-old woman develops massive postpartum hemorrhage complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation. Despite restoration of blood pressure, she remains anuric for 4 days and her serum creatinine continues to rise. Contrast-enhanced CT shows absent enhancement of most of the renal cortex with relative preservation of medullary enhancement.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis can follow shock but typically does not produce the characteristic cortical nonenhancement with relative medullary sparing.
Papillary necrosis affects the renal papillae/medulla and is associated with analgesics, diabetes, sickle cell disease, or severe pyelonephritis rather than diffuse cortical nonenhancement.
Bilateral renal artery stenosis causes renovascular disease and does not produce the classic postpartum/DIC cortical-necrosis imaging pattern.
Acute interstitial nephritis is an inflammatory tubulointerstitial process commonly associated with drug exposure and does not cause diffuse cortical necrosis.
key_expl: Persistent anuria after an obstetric catastrophe with DIC and imaging showing cortical nonenhancement with relative medullary sparing is classic for renal cortical necrosis. The lesion reflects severe cortical microvascular ischemia and thrombosis.
objective: Recognize renal cortical necrosis from persistent severe AKI/anuria after obstetric hemorrhage or DIC and characteristic cortical ischemic imaging.
